source_text: Venio nunc ad proprias Romanorum religiones, quoniam de communibus dixi. Romuli nutrix Lupa honoribus est adfecta diuinis, et ferrem, si animal ipsum, cuius figuram gerit. sed auctor est Liuius Larentinae esse simulacrum et quidem non corporis, sed mentis ac morum. fuit enim Faustuli uxor et propter uulgati corporis uilitatem lupa inter pastores id est meretrix nuncupata est; unde etiam lupanar dicitur. exemplum scilicet Atheniensium in ea figuranda Romani secuti sunt, apud quos meretrix quaedam nomine Leaena cum tyrannum occidisset, quia nefas erat simulacrum constitui meretricis in templo, animalis effigiem posuerunt cuius nomen gerebat. itaque ut illi monumentum ex nomine, sic isti ex professione fecerunt. huius nomini etiam dies festus dicatus est et Larentinalia constituta. nec hanc solam Romani meretricem colunt, sed Faulam quoque, quam Herculis scortum fuisse Verrius scribit. iam quanta ista inmortalitas putanda est, quam etiam meretrices adsecuntur? Flora cum magnas opes ex [ arte meretricia quaesiuisset., populum scripsit heredem certamque pecuniam reliquit, cuius ex annuo faenore suus natalis dies celebraretur editione ludorum, quos appellant Floralia. quod quia senatui flagitiosum uidebatur, ab ipso nomine argumentum sumi placuit, ut pudendae rei quaedam dignitas adderetur. deam finxerunt esse quae floribus praesit eamque oportere placari, ut fruges cum arboribus aut uitibus bene prospereque florescerent. eum colorem secutus in Fastis poeta non ignobilem nympham fuisse narrauit quae sit Chloris uocitata eamque Zephyro nuptam quasi dotis loco id accepisse muneris a marito, ut haberet florum omnium potestatem. honeste quidem ista dicuntur, sed inhoneste turpiterque creduntur nec debent, cum ueritas quaeritur, huiusmodi nos uelamenta decipere. celebrantur ergo illi ludi conuenienter memoriae meretricis cum omni lasciuia. nam praeter uerborum licentiam, quibus obscenitas omnis effunditur, exuuntur etiam uestibus populo flagitante meretrices, quae tunc mimarum funguntur officio et in conspectu populi usque ad satietatem inpudicorum luminum cum pudendis motibus detinentur. Cloacinae simulacrum in Cloaca Maxima repertum Tatius consecrauit et quia cuius esset effigies ignorabat, ex loco illi nomen inposuit. Pauorem Palloremque Tullus Hostilius figurauit et coluit. quid de hoc dicam nisi dignum fuisse qui semper deos suos, sicut optari solet, praesentes haberet? ab hoc illut Marci Marcelli de consecratione Honoris atque Virtutis honestate nominum differt, re congruit. eadem uanitate Mentem quoque inter deos senatus conlocauit, quam profecto si habuisset, eiusmodi sacra numquam suscepisset. magnum Cicero audaxque consilium suscepisse Graeciam dicit, quod Cupidinum et Amorum simulacra in gymnasiis consecrasset: adulatus est uidelicet Attico et inrisit hominem familiarem. non enim magnum illut aut omnino consilium dicendum fuit, sed inpudicorum hominum perdita et deplorata nequitia, qui liberos suos, quos erudire ad honestatem deberent, prostituerunt libidini iuuentutis: a quibus flagitiorum deos et in illis potissimum locis, ubi nuda corpora corruptorum luminibus patent, et in illa coli aetate uoluerunt, quae simplex et inprouida prius inretiri et in laqueos potest cadere quam cauere. quid mirum si ab hac gente uniuersa flagitia manarunt, aput quam uitia ipsa religiosa sunt eaque non modo non uitantur, uerum etiam coluntur? et ideo huic sententiae, tamquam Graecos prudentia uinceret, adiecit: uirtutes enim oportere, non uitia consecrari. quod si recipis, o Marce Tulli, non uides fore ut inrumpant uitia cum uirtutibus, quia mala bonis adhaerent, et in animis hominum potentiora sunt? quae si uetas consecrari, respondebit tibi eadem illa Graecia se alios deos colere ut prosint, alios uero ne noceant. haec enim semper excusatio est eorum qui mala sua pro diis habent, ut Romani robiginem ac febrem. si ergo uitia consecranda non sunt, in quo tibi adsentior, ne uirtutes quidem. non enim per se sapiunt aut sentiunt neque intra parietes aut aediculas luto factas, sed intra pectus collocandae sunt et interius conprehendendae, ne sint falsae, si extra hominem fuerint collocatae. itaque praeclaram illam legem tuam derideo quam ponis his uerbis: ast olla, propter quae datur homini ascensus in caelum, Mentem Virtutem Pietatem Fidem: earumque laudum delubra sunto. atquin haec separari ab homine non possunt. si enim colenda sunt, in homine ipso sint necesse est. si autem sint extra hominem, quid opus est ea colere quibus careas? uirtus enim colenda est, non imago uirtutis, et colenda est non sacrificio aliquo aut ture aut precatione sollemni, sed uoluntate sola atque proposito. nam quid est aliut colere uirtutem nisi eam conprehendere animo ac tenere? quod unus quisque simulac coepit uelle, consequitur. hic solus uirtutis est cultus: nam religio ac ueneratio nulla alia nisi unius dei tenenda est. quid igitur opus est, o uir sapientissime, superuacuis extructionibus loca occupare quae possint humanis usibus cedere? quid sacerdotes constituere uana et insensibilia culturos? quid immolare uictimas? quid tantos sumptus uel fingendis uel colendis imaginibus inpendere? firmius et incorruptius templum est pectus humanum: hoc potius ornetur, hoc ueris illis numinibus inpleatur. has ergo falsas consecrationes sequitur quod necesse est. qui enim sic uirtutes colunt id est qui umbras et imagines uirtutum consectantur, ea ipsa quae uera sunt tenere non possunt. itaque nulla in quoquam uirtus est, uitiis ubique dominantibus, nulla fides, omnia pro se quoque rapiente, nulla pietas, nec consanguineis nec parentibus parcente auaritia et cupiditate in uenena et in ferrum ruente, nulla pax, nulla concordia, publice bellis saeuientibus, priuatim uero inimicitiis usque ad sanguinem furentibus, nulla pudicitia, libidinibus effrenatis omnem sexum et omnes corporis partes contaminantibus. nec tamen desinunt ea colere quae fugiunt et oderunt. colunt enim ture ac summis digitis quae sensibus intimis horrere debuerunt: qui error omnis ex illius principalis ac summi boni ignoratione descendit. urbe a Gallis occupata obsessi in Capitolio Romani cum ex mulierum capillis tormenta fecissent, aedem Veneri Caluae consecrarunt. non igitur intellegunt, quam uanae sint religiones uel ex eo ipso, quod eas his ineptiis cauillantur. a Lacedaemoniis fortasse didicerant deos sibi ex euentis fingere. qui cum Messenios obsiderent et illi furtim deceptis obsessoribus egressi ad diripiendam Lacedaemonem cucurrissent, a Spartanis mulieribus fusi fugatique sunt. cognitis autem dolis hostium Lacedaemonii sequebantur. his armatae mulieres obuiam longius exierunt. quae cum uiros suos cernerent parare se ad pugnam, quod putarent Messenios esse, corpora sua nudauerunt. at illi uxoribus cognitis et aspectu in libidinem concitati, sicuti erant armati permixti sunt, utique promisce — nec enim uacabat discernere — sicut iuuenes ab isdem antea missi cum uirginibus, ex quibus sunt Partheniae nati. propter huius facti memoriam aedem Veneri Armatae simulacrumque posuerunt: quod tametsi ex causa turpi uenit, tamen honestius uidetur armatam Venerem consecrasse quam caluam. eodem tempore Ioui quoque Pistori ara posita est, quod eos in quiete monuisset, ut ex omni frumento quod habebant panem facerent et in hostium castra iactarent: eoque facto soluta esset obsidio desperantibus Gallis inopia subigi posse Romanos. quae ista religionum derisio est? si earum defensor essem, quid tam grauiter queri possem quam deorum numen in tantum uenisse contemptum, ut turpissimis nominibus ludibrio habeatur? quis non rideat Fornacem deam uel ; potius doctos uiros celebrandis Fornacalibus operari? quis cum audiat deam Mutam, tenere risum queat? hanc esse dicunt ex qua sint Lares nati et ipsam Laram nominant uel Larundam. quid praestare colenti potest quae loqui non potest? colitur et (Jaca, quae Herculi fecit indicium de turto boum, diuinitatem consecuta quia prodidit fratrem, et Cunina, quae infantes tuetur in cunis ac fascinum submouet, et Stercutus, qui stercorandi agri rationem primus induxit, et Tutinus, in cuius sinu pudendo nubentes praesident, ut illarum pudicitiam prior deus delibasse uideatur, et mille alia portenta, ut iam uaniores qui haec colenda susceperint quam Aegyptios esse dicamus, qui monstruosa et ridicula quaedam simulacra uenerantur. et haec tamen habent aliquam imaginem. quid qui lapidem colunt informem ac rudem cui nomen est Terminus? hic est quem pro Ioue Saturnus dicitur deuorasse nec inmerito illi honos tribuitur. nam cum Tarquinius Capitolium facere uellet atque in eo loco multorum deorum sacella essent, consuluit eos per auguria utrum Ioui cederent, et cedentibus ceteris solus Terminus mansit. unde illum poeta Capitoli inmobile saxum uocat. lam ex hoc ipso quam magnus Iuppiter inuenitur, cui non cessit lapis, ea fortasse fiducia, quod illum de paternis faucibus liberauerat. facto itaque Capitolio supra ipsum Terminum foramen est in tecto relictum, ut quia non cesserat, libero caelo frueretur: quo ne ipsi quidem fruebantur qui lapidem frui putauerunt.. et. huic ergo publice supplicatur quasi custodi finium deo, qui non tantum lapis, sed etiam stipes interdum est. quid de ns dicas qui colunt talia nisi ipsos potissimum lapides ac stipites esse?
pass_a_gloss: I come now to the Roman religions, since I spoke about the common ones. The nurse of Romulus, Lupa, is affected with divine honors, and also the iron, if it is the animal itself, whose figure it bears. But Livy is the author that the simulacrum of Larentia exists and indeed not of the body, but of the mind and morals. For she was the wife of Faustulus and because of the vileness of the common body, a prostitute was called Lupa among the shepherds; whence also the lupanar is called. The Romans followed the example of the Athenians in figuring this, among whom a certain prostitute named Leaena, when she had killed the tyrant, because it was a crime to set up a simulacrum of a prostitute in the temple, they placed the effigy of an animal whose name she bore. Thus, just as they made a monument from the name, so the Romans made it from the profession. A festive day is also dedicated to this name and the Larentinalia are established. Nor do the Romans worship only this prostitute, but also Faula, whom Verrius writes was the mistress of Hercules. How great is this immortality to be considered, which even prostitutes attain? Flora, when she had acquired great wealth from the art of prostitution, wrote the people as her heir and left a certain amount of money, from whose annual interest her birthday would be celebrated with the production of games, which they call Floralia. Because this seemed shameful to the senate, it was decided to take an argument from the name itself, so that some dignity would be added to the shameful thing. They feigned that she was a goddess who presided over flowers and that she should be placated, so that the crops with trees or vines would flourish well and prosperously. The poet, following this color, narrated in the Fasti that she was not an ignoble nymph, but one who was called Chloris and was married to Zephyr, and that she received as a gift from her husband the power of all flowers. These things are said honorably, but they are believed shamefully and turpishly and should not be, when the truth is sought, and we should not be deceived by such veils. Therefore, those games are celebrated conveniently in memory of the prostitute with all lasciviousness. For besides the license of words, with which all obscenity is poured out, prostitutes also strip themselves of their clothes, with the people demanding it, and they perform the function of mimics and are detained in the sight of the people with shameful movements until they are satisfied. The simulacrum of Cloacina was found in the Cloaca Maxima and consecrated by Tatius, and because he did not know whose effigy it was, he gave it a name from the place. Tullus Hostilius figured and worshiped Pavor and Pallor. What should I say about this, except that it was worthy of one who always had his gods present, as is usually desired? This differs from the consecration of Honor and Virtue by Marcus Marcellus in the honesty of the names, but it agrees in the thing itself. The senate also placed Mind among the gods with the same vanity, which, if they had possessed, they would never have undertaken such sacrifices. Cicero says that the Greeks had a bold and daring plan, because they had consecrated simulacra of Cupids and Loves in the gymnasia: he was clearly flattering Atticus and mocking a familiar man. For this was not a great or even a plan at all, but the lost and deplorable wickedness of shameless men, who prostituted their children, whom they should have educated in honesty, to the lust of youth: from whom they wanted the gods of shameful things to be worshiped, and in those places, where the naked bodies of the corrupt are exposed to the eyes, and in that age, which is simple and inexperienced, and can be caught in snares before it can beware. What is surprising, if all shameful things flowed from this people, among whom vices themselves are religious and are not only not avoided, but even worshiped? And therefore he added to this sentence, as if the Greeks were surpassed by prudence: for virtues should be consecrated, not vices. But if you accept this, O Marcus Tullius, do you not see that vices will burst in with virtues, because evils cling to goods, and are more powerful in the minds of men? Which, if you forbid to be consecrated, Greece will respond to you that they worship some gods so that they may be helpful, and others so that they may not harm. For this is always the excuse of those who have their evils as gods, as the Romans have rust and fever. If, therefore, vices should not be consecrated, which I agree with, then not even virtues should be. For they do not have wisdom or feeling in themselves, nor are they enclosed within walls or little houses made of mud, but they should be placed in the heart and comprehended inwardly, lest they be false, if they are placed outside of man. Therefore, I deride that famous law of yours, which you propose in these words: 'But, O man, for whom ascension to heaven is given, let there be temples of Mind, Virtue, Piety, and Faith.' But these cannot be separated from man. For if they are to be worshiped, they must necessarily be in man himself. If, however, they are outside of man, what need is there to worship them, when you lack them? For virtue should be worshiped, not the image of virtue, and it should be worshiped not with some sacrifice or incense or solemn prayer, but with the will alone and the intention. For what is it to worship virtue, except to comprehend it with the mind and to hold it? Which each person achieves as soon as he begins to will it. This alone is the worship of virtue: for no religion or veneration should be held except that of the one God. What need is there, O wisest man, to occupy places with superfluous buildings, which can yield to human uses? What need is there to establish priests who will worship vain and insensible things? What need is there to immolate victims? What need is there to spend so much on fabricating or worshiping images? The human heart is a stronger and more incorruptible temple: this should be adorned, this should be filled with true divinities. These false consecrations follow necessarily. For those who worship virtues in this way, that is, who pursue the shadows and images of virtues, cannot hold the true ones. Thus, there is no virtue in anyone, with vices dominating everywhere, no faith, with everyone seizing everything for himself, no piety, with avarice and cupidity rushing into poison and the sword, not sparing even relatives or parents, no peace, no concord, with public wars raging and private enmities burning up to bloodshed, no chastity, with unbridled lusts contaminating every sex and every part of the body. And yet they do not cease to worship those things which they flee from and hate. For they worship with incense and the highest digits those things which they should abhor with their inner senses: which error descends from the ignorance of the principal and highest good. When the Romans were besieged in the Capitol by the Gauls and had made catapults from women's hair, they consecrated a temple to Venus Calva. Therefore, they do not understand how vain their religions are, even from the fact that they mock them with such foolishness. Perhaps they learned from the Lacedaemonians to feign gods for themselves from events. When the Lacedaemonians were besieging the Messenians and the Messenians had secretly deceived the besiegers and had run out to plunder Lacedaemon, they were put to flight by the Spartan women. When the Lacedaemonians recognized the deceit of the enemy, they followed them. The armed women went out to meet them from a distance. When they saw their husbands preparing for battle, thinking they were Messenians, they uncovered their bodies. And the men, recognizing their wives and excited by the sight to lust, mixed with them, armed as they were, promiscuously - for there was no time to distinguish - just as the young men who had been sent earlier with the virgins, from whom the Partheniae were born. In memory of this deed, they set up a temple and simulacrum to Venus Armata: which, although it came from a shameful cause, seems more honorable than consecrating Venus Calva. At the same time, an altar was placed to Jupiter the Baker, because he had warned them in quiet to make bread from all the grain they had and to throw it into the camp of the enemy: and by doing this, the siege was lifted, with the Gauls despairing that the Romans could be subdued by lack of supplies. What mockery of religions is this? If I were a defender of them, what could I complain about more seriously than that the numen of the gods has come to such contempt, that it is held in ridicule by the most shameful names? Who would not laugh at Fornax, the goddess of the oven, or rather at learned men celebrating the Fornacalia? Who could restrain laughter when hearing about the goddess Muta? They say she is the one from whom the Lares were born, and they call her Laram or Larunda. What can she provide to the one who worships her, when she cannot speak? They also worship Iaca, who gave indication to Hercules about the theft of the oxen, and who attained divinity because she betrayed her brother, and Cunina, who protects infants in their cradles and removes the evil eye, and Stercutus, who first introduced the method of fertilizing the fields, and Tutinus, in whose shameful lap the newlyweds sit, so that it may seem that the god had first tasted their chastity, and a thousand other monstrous things, so that we may say that those who undertook to worship these things are more foolish than the Egyptians, who worship monstrous and ridiculous simulacra. And yet these have some image. What about those who worship an unformed and rude stone, whose name is Terminus? This is the one whom Saturn is said to have devoured, and not undeservedly is honor paid to him. For when Tarquinius wanted to build the Capitol, and there were sacella of many gods in that place, he consulted them through auguries whether they would yield to Jupiter, and when the others yielded, Terminus alone remained. Whence the poet calls him the immovable rock of the Capitol. Now from this very thing, how great Jupiter is found to be, to whom not even a stone yielded, perhaps with the confidence that he had freed him from the paternal jaws. Therefore, when the Capitol was built, a hole was left in the roof above Terminus, so that because he had not yielded, he might enjoy the free sky: which not even those who thought the stone enjoyed it, enjoyed themselves. And therefore, public supplication is made to him as if to the guardian god of boundaries, who is not only a stone, but sometimes also a stake. What should we say about those who worship such things, except that they themselves are rather stones and stakes?

pass_b_english: I turn now to Rome's own cults, having already addressed the common ones. Divine honors were bestowed on the wolf that nursed Romulus — and one might accept that, if the actual animal were the object of worship. But Livy records that the image honored was not the wolf's body but the mind and character of Larentia. She was Faustulus' wife, and because of the shame attached to her body, the shepherds called her 'Lupa' — that is, a prostitute; hence the word 'lupanar' for a brothel. The Romans followed the Athenian precedent in shaping this figure: when the prostitute Leaena killed a tyrant at Athens, they could not lawfully erect her statue in a temple, so they set up an effigy of the animal whose name she bore. Thus the Athenians made a monument from a name; the Romans made one from a profession. A feast day was dedicated to her name, and the Larentalia were instituted. Nor do the Romans worship only this prostitute; they also worship Faula, whom Verrius records as the mistress of Hercules. What kind of immortality is this that even harlots attain? Flora, after amassing great wealth through prostitution, made the Roman people her heir and left a sum whose annual interest would fund games on her birthday — the games called Floralia. The Senate found this shameful, so it was decided to derive a pretext from the name itself, to lend some dignity to a disgraceful thing. They invented a goddess presiding over flowers who must be placated so that crops, trees, and vines might flourish. The poet in the Fasti followed this coloring, telling how a noble nymph named Chloris, wed to Zephyr, received from her husband the dominion over all flowers as a bridal gift. The story is told honorably, but it is believed shamefully and basely; such veils must not deceive us when we seek the truth. Accordingly those games are celebrated with all lasciviousness, fittingly commemorating a harlot. For beyond the license of speech that pours out every obscenity, prostitutes strip naked at the crowd's demand, act as mimes, and are held in public view with shameful movements until the spectators are sated. Tatius consecrated the image of Cloacina, found in the Cloaca Maxima; ignorant of whose likeness it was, he named her from the place. Tullus Hostilius fashioned and worshiped Pavor and Pallor. What can one say of this, except that it befitted a man who always kept his gods at hand, as people commonly wish? This differs from Marcus Marcellus' consecration of Honor and Virtue in the honesty of the names, yet agrees in the substance. The Senate, in the same vanity, placed Mind among the gods — a Mind which, if they truly possessed it, would never have led them to undertake such rites. Cicero calls it a bold and great design of the Greeks to have consecrated images of Cupids and Loves in the gymnasia; he was plainly flattering Atticus and mocking a friend. For it was neither great nor a design at all, but the lost and desperate wickedness of shameless men who prostituted their own children — whom they ought to have trained in honor — to the lust of youth. From such men came the demand that gods of shame be worshiped precisely in those places where naked bodies lie exposed to corrupt eyes, and at that age which is simple and unwary, more easily caught in snares than able to guard against them. What wonder if every vice flowed from a people among whom vices themselves are religious — not only not avoided, but actually worshiped? Therefore Cicero added, as if the Greeks excelled in prudence: 'Virtues ought to be consecrated, not vices.' But if you accept that, Marcus Tullius, do you not see that vices will burst in alongside virtues, because evils cling to goods and are more powerful in human minds? And if you forbid the consecration of vices, Greece will answer that she worships some gods to gain their help, others to avert their harm — the perpetual excuse of those who make their evils into gods, as the Romans do with Rust and Fever. So if vices are not to be consecrated — a point I grant — then neither should virtues. For virtues do not possess wisdom or feeling in themselves, nor do they dwell within walls or mud-built shrines; they must be lodged in the heart and grasped inwardly, lest they become false when placed outside a man. Therefore I mock that famous law of yours which you phrase thus: 'But for the man to whom ascent to heaven is given, let there be temples of Mind, Virtue, Piety, Faith.' Yet these cannot be separated from man. If they are to be worshiped, they must exist in man himself. If they exist outside him, what use is it to worship what you lack? Virtue is to be worshiped, not the image of virtue; and it is to be worshiped not by sacrifice, incense, or formal prayer, but by will and purpose alone. For what is worshiping virtue except comprehending it with the mind and holding it fast? Each person achieves this the moment he begins to will it. This alone is the worship of virtue: for no religion or reverence is due except to the one God. Why then, wisest of men, occupy space with superfluous buildings that could serve human needs? Why appoint priests to tend vain and senseless things? Why immolate victims? Why spend such sums fabricating and worshiping images? The human heart is a stronger and more incorruptible temple: let it be adorned, let it be filled with true divinities. These false consecrations follow of necessity. For those who worship virtues this way — that is, who chase shadows and images of virtues — cannot hold the true virtues themselves. Hence there is no virtue in anyone, vices reigning everywhere; no faith, each seizing everything for himself; no piety, greed and lust driving men to poison and the sword, sparing neither kin nor parents; no peace, no concord, public wars raging and private hatreds flaming to bloodshed; no chastity, unbridled lusts defiling every sex and every part of the body. And yet they do not cease to worship the very things they flee and hate. They offer incense and the pinch of fingertips to things they ought to abhor with their inmost senses — an error springing from ignorance of the highest and chief Good. When the Gauls occupied the city and the Romans were besieged on the Capitol, they made catapults from women's hair and consecrated a temple to Venus Calva. Thus they do not perceive how empty their religions are, even from the fact that they mock them with such follies. Perhaps they learned from the Lacedaemonians to invent gods from events. When the Lacedaemonians besieged the Messenians, and the Messenians slipped out by deceit to plunder Lacedaemon, they were routed by Spartan women. The Lacedaemonians, discovering the trick, pursued. Armed women went out to meet them at a distance. Seeing their husbands preparing for battle, thinking them Messenians, the women bared their bodies. The men, recognizing their wives and inflamed to lust, mingled with them promiscuously, still armed — there was no time to distinguish — just as the young men sent earlier with the virgins, from whom the Partheniae were born. In memory of this deed they erected a temple and image to Venus Armata: which, though born of a shameful cause, seems more honorable than consecrating Venus Calva. At the same time an altar was set up to Jupiter the Baker, because he had warned them in a quiet moment to bake all their grain into bread and throw it into the enemy camp; this done, the siege was lifted, the Gauls despairing of starving the Romans. What mockery of religion is this? If I were its defender, what could I complain of more gravely than that the divine numen has sunk to such contempt as to be ridiculed by the most shameful names? Who would not laugh at Fornax the oven-goddess, or rather at learned men busying themselves with the Fornacalia? Who can keep from laughter on hearing of the goddess Muta? They say she is the mother of the Lares, and call her Lara or Larunda. What can she grant a worshipper who cannot speak? They also worship Iaca, who betrayed her brother to Hercules about the cattle theft and won divinity for her treachery; and Cunina, who guards infants in cradles and averts the evil eye; and Stercutus, who first taught the art of manuring fields; and Tutinus, in whose shameful lap brides sit, as if the god must first taste their chastity; and a thousand other monsters — so that we might say those who undertook to worship these are more foolish than the Egyptians, who venerate monstrous and ridiculous images. Even those have some semblance. What of those who worship an unshaped, rude stone named Terminus? This is the stone Saturn is said to have swallowed, and not without reason is he honored. When Tarquinius wished to build the Capitol, many gods' shrines stood on the site; he consulted them by augury whether they would yield to Jupiter. The others yielded; Terminus alone stood fast. Hence the poet calls him the immovable rock of the Capitol. From this very fact we see how great Jupiter is — to whom not even a stone yielded, perhaps trusting that he had freed it from his father's jaws. So when the Capitol was built, a hole was left in the roof above Terminus, that he might enjoy the open sky since he had not yielded — a sky which not even those who thought the stone enjoyed it could enjoy themselves. Public supplication is therefore made to him as guardian of boundaries, though he is not only a stone but sometimes a mere stake. What can we say of those who worship such things, except that they themselves are rather stones and stakes?
notes: The text is a critique of Roman religions and the worship of various gods and goddesses, including Larentia, Virtus, and Cupido. The author argues that these gods are not worthy of worship and that the Romans are foolish to believe in them.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the nuances of the author's polemic. All specific mythological references (Lupa, Larentia, Flora, Chloris, Cloacina, Pavor, Pallor, Venus Calva/Armata, Jupiter Pistori, Fornax, Muta, Iaca, Cunina, Stercutus, Tutinus, Terminus) and the philosophical arguments regarding the nature of virtue and the heart as a temple are faithfully rendered in both Pass A and Pass B. The distinction between the 'simulacrum' of the body and the 'mentis ac morum' is correctly handled. The translation of the Cicero quote and the subsequent debate on whether vices or virtues should be consecrated is precise.
